Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

issues.item: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Hard to Recall Deliberately' conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' Deliberate retrieval difficulty and very easy verbal access are opposing states and are hard to reconcile as describing the same patient at the same time, especially alongside 'Overwhelm on Recall,' which implies traumatic recall is effortful and dysregulating rather than easy to discuss.

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' directly conflicts with 'When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop.' At this severity level and with strong Trigger↔Memory and Memory→Threat links, these two memory items describe opposing levels of accessibility/distress and are hard to reconcile as the same current presentation.

issues.item: Triggers: Authority Commands: Being given orders or instructions
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile with stalking as the index trauma: 'authority commands' and especially 'bicycle' do not show an evident clinical link to the reported trauma, and the profile provides no memory or appraisal content that would make these idiosyncratic triggers understandable.

Threat items emphasize broad interpersonal attack and generic danger vigilance (loud sounds, scanning exits, watching others for harm), which fits assault/combat/fire trauma better than stalking. For stalking, one would expect threat focused more on being followed, approached, monitored, contacted, or found by the perpetrator.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'I am a weak person' sits awkwardly with this profile and occupation unless supported by appraisal content about failure to protect oneself or family; here the other appraisals center on permanent damage and fear of going crazy, so the weakness item feels less coherent with the stalking-specific formulation than those items.

vignette: Tariq first felt the stalking crystallize in the hollowed silence of late November. He had been riding his bicycle down the eastern corridor of Meridian Park when the cadence of another set of tires synced with his own. He glanced over, catching the blur of a man who never accelerated past him, who appeared at every crosswalk, who seemed to know the shortcut alleys Tariq used to bypass traffic. The sensation of being tracked settled into his shoulders like lead. It culminated behind a condemned brick warehouse near the river, where the pavement narrowed into a dead end. Tariq braked, his breath pluming in the cold, certain that footsteps were closing in from the dark. When the figure finally stepped into the sodium glare, Tariq ran, his lungs burning, trapped by the certainty that the space itself had been engineered to contain him. The months that followed folded into a landscape of parallel tensions. Tariq could no longer pass the warehouse or the park's trail without his pulse quickening. Every unfamiliar alley, every closed gate, every stretch of pavement that ended abruptly felt charged with the memory of that narrowed corridor. When he tried to speak of the riverbank to his wife, Leila, the narrative would dissolve in his throat. He knew precisely what happened, yet he could not find the language to hold it. When the memory returned, a heavy, suffocating wave of emotion would strike, forcing him to stop speaking, to sit perfectly still until the pressure behind his eyes receded. He found that fragments of the past surfaced without warning: a car backfiring on Elm Street, the sudden screech of tires, or a shadow crossing his kitchen window would instantly pull him back to the dead end, leaving him standing in the present while his body braced for pursuit that had long since passed. His days as a firefighter demanded steadiness, yet his environment had turned into a field of constant assessment. In the apparatus bay, where radios crackled and hydraulic doors groaned, any unexpected loud sound made his shoulders snap upward, his breath catching as if he were still bracing for impact. He had come to believe that his body no longer trusted the ground beneath him. When entering any room, any station, any new building, his eyes automatically mapped the doors and windows. He watched others closely, not with animosity, but with a quiet, exhausting tally of their gestures, scanning for the shift in posture that preceded threat. The fatigue was absolute. What frightened him most was the erosion of his own mind. He was certain that his reactions meant he was going crazy, that the man who used to climb ladders and hold calm had permanently changed for the worse. Worse still was the conviction that he was weak. A firefighter who flinched at shadows shouldn't be carrying this. He stopped riding his bicycle to work, taking long, circuitous bus routes instead, though the rattling seats and sudden stops only sharpened his fear of being followed. He avoided the park entirely. Leila had begun to notice the distance in his voice, the way he flinched when he thought he wasn't being watched. The avoidance had carved quiet spaces into his weeks, but it had also carved him. His gear hung heavier. His shifts felt longer. The consequences of staying vigilant were no longer abstract; they were in the missed conversations, the tense silence at the dinner table, the way he counted the exits in his own living room. He finally walked into the clinic because he could no longer separate the threat from the present. He was hoping to find a way to ride his bicycle again without bracing for pursuit, to speak of the riverbank without his voice giving out. What he feared most was not the past returning, but waking up to find that he had already lost himself, that the man he was before had been irrevocably broken, and that he would spend the rest of his life scanning for doors he never needed to leave.
